results.title: $p$-soluble groups
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $p$ be a natural number. A group $G$ is $p$-soluble when it has a subnormal series $1 = H_0 \le H_1 \le \dots \le H_n = G$, each $H_i$ normal in $H_{i+1}$, whose factors $H_{i+1}/H_i$ are $p$-groups or have order prime to $p$. Here an infinite factor is taken to have order $0$.

results.title: Groups with a $p$-block of defect zero
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $p$ be a natural number. A group $G$ has a $p$-block of defect zero when some irreducible finite-dimensional complex representation of $G$ has degree divisible by $p^{v_p(|G|)}$, where $v_p(|G|)$ is the exponent of $p$ in the prime factorization of the order $|G|$ of $G$ (this exponent is $0$ when $p$ is not prime or $G$ is infinite). For a prime $p$ and a finite group $G$, the number $p^{v_p(|G|)}$ is $|G|_p$,…

results.title: Kourovka Problem 12.26
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: This is the proposition (Shi Shengming) that for every prime $p$ and every finite $p$-soluble group $G$, the group $G$ has a $p$-block of defect zero if and only if some normal subgroup $N$ of $G$ of order prime to $p$ contains an element $x$ whose centralizer $C_G(x)$ in $G$ has order prime to $p$.

results.title: Refutation of Kourovka Problem 12.26
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The proposition of Kourovka Problem 12.26 is false: it is not the case that for every prime $p$ and every finite $p$-soluble group $G$, the group $G$ has a $p$-block of defect zero if and only if some normal subgroup $N$ of $G$ of order prime to $p$ contains an element $x$ whose centralizer $C_G(x)$ in $G$ has order prime to $p$.

results.title: Characters of $p$-defect zero
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $p$ and a group $G$, the set of characters $\chi \colon G \to \mathbb{C}$ of irreducible finite-dimensional complex representations of $G$ whose degree is divisible by $p^a$, where $a$ is the exponent of $p$ in the prime factorization of the order $|G|$ (and $a = 0$ when $G$ is infinite or $p$ is not prime).

results.title: Number of solutions of a commutator equation
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For an element $g$ of a group $G$, the number of pairs $(x, y) \in G \times G$ with $[x, y] = x y x^{-1} y^{-1} = g$, taken to be $0$ when there are infinitely many such pairs.

results.title: Conjugacy classes with commutator count not divisible by $p$
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $p$ and a group $G$, the set of conjugacy classes of $G$ containing an element $g$ such that the number of pairs $(x, y) \in G \times G$ with $[x, y] = x y x^{-1} y^{-1} = g$ (taken to be $0$ when there are infinitely many) is not divisible by $p$.

results.title: Kourovka Problem 12.80(a): blocks of defect zero and commutator equations
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For every prime $p$ and every finite group $G$ whose order is divisible by $p$, the number of irreducible complex characters of $G$ of $p$-defect zero equals the number of conjugacy classes of $G$ containing an element $g$ for which the number of pairs $(x, y) \in G \times G$ with $[x, y] = x y x^{-1} y^{-1} = g$ is not divisible by $p$.

results.title: Kourovka Problem 12.80(b): the case of simple groups
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For every prime $p$ and every finite simple group $G$ whose order is divisible by $p$, the number of irreducible complex characters of $G$ of $p$-defect zero equals the number of conjugacy classes of $G$ containing an element $g$ for which the number of pairs $(x, y) \in G \times G$ with $[x, y] = x y x^{-1} y^{-1} = g$ is not divisible by $p$.

results.title: Kourovka Problem 12.80(a) has a negative answer
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: It is not true that for every prime $p$ and every finite group $G$ whose order is divisible by $p$, the number of irreducible complex characters of $G$ of $p$-defect zero equals the number of conjugacy classes of $G$ containing an element $g$ for which the number of pairs $(x, y) \in G \times G$ with $[x, y] = x y x^{-1} y^{-1} = g$ is not divisible by $p$.

results.title: Kourovka Problem 12.80(b) has a negative answer
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: It is not true that for every prime $p$ and every finite simple group $G$ whose order is divisible by $p$, the number of irreducible complex characters of $G$ of $p$-defect zero equals the number of conjugacy classes of $G$ containing an element $g$ for which the number of pairs $(x, y) \in G \times G$ with $[x, y] = x y x^{-1} y^{-1} = g$ is not divisible by $p$.

results.title: Multiplicity of an indexed system of residue classes

results.summary: Given $k \in \mathbb{N}$, moduli $m_0, \dots, m_{k-1} \in \mathbb{N}$ and residues $r_0, \dots, r_{k-1} \in \mathbb{Z}$, the multiplicity of an integer $z$ is the number of indices $i < k$ with $z \equiv r_i \pmod{m_i}$.

results.title: Greatest common monic divisor
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $h, g_1, g_2 \in R[x]$. Then $h$ is a greatest common monic divisor of $g_1$ and $g_2$ when $h$, $g_1$ and $g_2$ are monic and the ideal generated by $g_1$ and $g_2$ equals the principal ideal generated by $h$.

results.title: Unfolding the greatest common monic divisor
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For polynomials $h$, $g_1$ and $g_2$ over a commutative ring $R$, $h$ is a greatest common monic divisor of $g_1$ and $g_2$ if and only if $h$, $g_1$ and $g_2$ are monic and the ideal of $R[X]$ generated by $g_1$ and $g_2$ equals the principal ideal generated by $h$.

results.title: Frobenius pseudoprime
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A natural number $n$ is a Frobenius pseudoprime with respect to a polynomial $f \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ when $n$ is not prime and $n$ is a Frobenius probable prime with respect to $f$.

results.title: Characterization of Frobenius probable primes

Then $n$ is a Frobenius probable prime with respect to $f$ if and only if $f$ is monic, $n$ is odd, $n > 1$, $n$ is coprime to $|f(0)\Delta|$, and there exist polynomials $F_i, f_i \in (\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})[x]$ and natural numbers $q_i$, indexed by $i \in \mathbb{N}$, such that: and $f_{i-1}$, and…

results.title: Frobenius probable primes use monic polynomials
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $n$ is a Frobenius probable prime with respect to a polynomial $f \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$, then $f$ is monic.

results.title: Frobenius probable primes are odd
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $n$ is a Frobenius probable prime with respect to a polynomial $f \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$, then $n$ is odd.

results.title: Frobenius probable primes exceed one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $n$ is a Frobenius probable prime with respect to a polynomial $f \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$, then $n > 1$.

results.title: Characterization of Frobenius pseudoprimes
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n$ and every polynomial $f \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$, $n$ is a Frobenius pseudoprime with respect to $f$ if and only if $n$ is not prime and $n$ is a Frobenius probable prime with respect to $f$.

results.title: Frobenius pseudoprimes are not prime
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $n$ is a Frobenius pseudoprime with respect to a polynomial $f \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$, then $n$ is not prime.

results.title: Frobenius pseudoprimes are Frobenius probable primes
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If $n$ is a Frobenius pseudoprime with respect to a polynomial $f \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$, then $n$ is a Frobenius probable prime with respect to $f$.

results.title: Points of the Euclidean plane
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: A planar point is a point of the Euclidean plane $\mathbb{R}^2$: a pair $(x, y)$ of real numbers, with the Euclidean norm $\lVert (x, y) \rVert = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}$.

results.title: Cyclic successor
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $n$ and an index $i$ with $0 \le i < n$, the cyclic successor of $i$ is $(i + 1) \bmod n$; in particular the successor of $n - 1$ is $0$. For $n = 0$ there are no indices.

results.title: Length of a closed tour
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For points $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ in the Euclidean plane and a permutation $\sigma$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, the tour length is $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} \lVert x_{\sigma(i)} - x_{\sigma(i+1 \bmod n)} \rVert$, the length of the closed tour that visits $x_{\sigma(0)}, \dots, x_{\sigma(n-1)}$ in this order and returns to its start.

results.title: Shortest tour length
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For points $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ in the Euclidean plane, $L_n$ is the minimum, over all permutations $\sigma$ of $\{0, \dots, n-1\}$, of the length of the closed tour that visits $x_{\sigma(0)}, \dots, x_{\sigma(n-1)}$ in this order and returns to its start.

results.title: Normalized tour length
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\Omega$ be a set and let $X_0, X_1, X_2, \dots \colon \Omega \to \mathbb{R}^2$ be functions. For an outcome $\omega \in \Omega$ and $n \ge 1$, the normalized tour length is $L_n(\omega)/\sqrt{n}$, where $L_n(\omega)$ is the length of a shortest closed tour through $X_0(\omega), \dots, X_{n-1}(\omega)$. For $n = 0$ it is defined to be $0$.

results.title: BHH limit values of a sampling law
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a measure $\mu$ on the plane, the BHH limit values of $\mu$ form the set of real numbers $\beta$ that are BHH limits for $\mu$.

results.title: Membership in the set of BHH limit values
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary:
For a measure $

results.title: Unique BHH constant of a law
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A measure $\nu$ on the plane has a unique BHH constant when there is exactly one real number $\beta$ that is a BHH constant for $\nu$.

results.title: BHH constant of a sampling law
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a measure $\mu$ on the plane, the BHH constant of $\mu$ is the infimum of the set of real numbers $\beta$ that are BHH limits for $\mu$. The infimum of a set of reals that is empty or not bounded below is taken to be $0$.

results.title: The BHH constant equals the unique BHH limit
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\mu$ be a measure on the plane and $\beta$ a real number. If, for every real $\gamma$, $\gamma$ is a BHH limit for $\mu$ if and only if $\gamma = \beta$, then the BHH constant of $\mu$ (the infimum of its BHH limits) equals $\beta$.

results.title: Unit square

results.title: Statement of the Beardwood–Halton–Hammersley upper bound
results.caption: Definition

results.title: Statement of the Beardwood–Halton–Hammersley lower bound
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: This is the proposition that the Beardwood–Halton–Hammersley constant $\beta_2$ for uniform points in the unit square satisfies $\beta_2 \ge 5/8 = 0.625$, the lower bound reported by Beardwood, Halton and Hammersley (1959).

results.title: Statement of the Gaudio–Jaillet lower bound
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The proposition that the Beardwood–Halton–Hammersley constant $\beta_2$ of the unit square is at least $0.6277$, that is, $0.6277 \le \beta_2$.

results.title: Erdős Problem 658 (axis-parallel squares in dense subsets of the grid)
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The statement that for every real number $\delta > 0$ there is a natural number $N_0$ such that for every $N \ge N_0$, every set $A \subseteq \{1, \dots, N\}^2$ of pairs of natural numbers with $|A| \ge \delta N^2$ contains the four vertices $(a, b)$, $(a + d, b)$, $(a, b + d)$ and $(a + d, b + d)$ of an axis-parallel square, for some natural numbers $a$, $b$ and $d \ge 1$.

results.title: Flag $f$-vector

results.title: Longest-path instances
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: A longest-path instance is a tuple $(n, E, K, s, t)$ consisting of a natural number $n$, the number of vertices; a list $E$ of pairs of natural numbers, the edges; and natural numbers $K$, the length bound, $s$, the start vertex, and $t$, the target vertex.

results.title: Graph of a longest-path instance
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a longest-path instance with vertex count $n$ and edge list $E$, its graph is the graph of the edge list $E$ on $n$ vertices: the simple graph on $\{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ in which distinct vertices $i$ and $j$ are adjacent when $(i, j)$ or $(j, i)$ belongs to $E$.

results.title: Well-formed longest-path instances
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A longest-path instance $(n, E, K, s, t)$ is well formed when $s < n$, $t < n$, the list $E$ has no repeated entries, and every pair $(u, v)$ in $E$ satisfies $u < n$, $v < n$ and $u \ne v$, and its reverse $(v, u)$ does not belong to $E$.

results.title: Feasibility of a longest-path instance
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A longest-path instance $(n, E, K, s, t)$ is feasible when the graph of $E$ on $n$ vertices has a simple path from $s$ to $t$ with at least $K$ edges, that is, a list $v_0, \dots, v_m$ of pairwise distinct vertices with $m \ge K$, $v_0 = s$ and $v_m = t$, in which $v_j$ and $v_{j+1}$ are adjacent for every $j < m$.

results.title: The LONGEST PATH decision problem
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: LONGEST PATH is the decision problem that accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding, to a longest-path instance $(n, E, K, s, t)$ that is well formed and in which the graph of $E$ on $n$ vertices has a simple path from $s$ to $t$ with at least $K$ edges. Bitstrings that do not decode to a longest-path instance are rejected.

results.title: LONGEST PATH is NP-complete
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The LONGEST PATH decision problem belongs to NP, and every decision problem in NP has a polynomial-time many-one reduction to LONGEST PATH.

results.title: Whether two context-free languages intersect is undecidable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There is an alphabet $T$, with decidable equality and a primitive recursive encoding into $\mathbb{N}$, such that no multi-stack machine decides (in the sense of TM2-decidability), for a pair $(G_1, G_2)$ of encoded context-free grammars over $T$, whether some word lies in both $L(G_1)$ and $L(G_2)$, where $L(G)$ is the language of $G$.

results.title: Whether two context-free languages are disjoint is undecidable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There is an alphabet $T$, with decidable equality and a primitive recursive encoding into $\mathbb{N}$, such that no multi-stack machine decides (in the sense of TM2-decidability), for a pair $(G_1, G_2)$ of encoded context-free grammars over $T$, whether no word lies in both $L(G_1)$ and $L(G_2)$, where $L(G)$ is the language of $G$.

results.title: Whether a context-free grammar is ambiguous is undecidable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There is an alphabet $T$, with decidable equality and a primitive recursive encoding into $\mathbb{N}$, such that no multi-stack machine decides (in the sense of TM2-decidability), for an encoded context-free grammar $G$ over $T$, whether $G$ is ambiguous, that is, whether some word has two different leftmost derivations from the start nonterminal of $G$.

results.title: Whether a context-free grammar generates every word is undecidable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There is a finite alphabet $T$, with decidable equality and a primitive recursive encoding into $\mathbb{N}$, such that no multi-stack machine decides (in the sense of TM2-decidability), for an encoded context-free grammar $G$ over $T$, whether every word over $T$ lies in the language of $G$.

results.title: Grammar of all words
results.caption: Definition

results.title: Equivalence of context-free grammars is undecidable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There is a finite alphabet $T$, with decidable equality and a primitive recursive encoding into $\mathbb{N}$, such that no multi-stack machine decides (in the sense of TM2-decidability), for a pair $(G_1, G_2)$ of encoded context-free grammars over $T$, whether $L(G_1) = L(G_2)$, where $L(G)$ is the language of $G$.

results.title: Inclusion of context-free languages is undecidable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There is a finite alphabet $T$, with decidable equality and a primitive recursive encoding into $\mathbb{N}$, such that no multi-stack machine decides (in the sense of TM2-decidability), for a pair $(G_1, G_2)$ of encoded context-free grammars over $T$, whether $L(G_1) \subseteq L(G_2)$, where $L(G)$ is the language of $G$.

results.title: Universality of context-free grammars is co-recognizable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every alphabet $T$ with a primcodable encoding and decidable equality, the set of encoded context-free grammars over $T$ whose language contains every word over $T$ is co-recognizable by a multi-stack Turing machine.

results.title: Disjointness of context-free languages is not recognizable

results.summary: There is an alphabet $T$, with a primcodable encoding and decidable equality, such that the set of pairs $(g_1, g_2)$ of encoded context-free grammars over $T$ whose languages are disjoint (no word lies in both) is not recognizable by a multi-stack Turing machine.

results.title: Universality of context-free grammars is not recognizable

results.title: The lower chain is a sublist of the input
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\Bbbk$ be a linearly ordered field and let $p_1, \dots, p_n$ be points of $\Bbbk^2$ that are strictly increasing in lexicographic $(x, y)$ order. Then the lower chain of $p_1, \dots, p_n$ is a sublist of $p_1, \dots, p_n$: it is $p_{i_1}, \dots, p_{i_m}$ for some indices $i_1 < \dots < i_m$.

results.title: Upper chain
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $K$ be a field with a linear order. The upper chain of a list of points $p_1, \dots, p_n \in K^2$ is the lower chain of the reversed list $p_n, \dots, p_1$, together with its cost: the same scan, counting the same orientation tests. For points sorted by $(x, y)$ it runs from the last point back to the first.

results.title: Convex hull by the monotone chain algorithm
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\Bbbk$ be a field with a linear order. The convex hull of a list $P$ of points of $\Bbbk^2$ is the lower chain of $P$ followed by the upper chain of $P$ with its first and last points removed, together with its cost: the cost of computing the lower chain plus the cost of computing the upper chain.

results.title: The upper chain is a reflected lower chain
results.caption: Theorem

results.title: The upper chain is a subsequence of the reversed input

Then the upper chain of $p_1, \dots, p_n$ is a sublist of the reversed list $p_n, \dots, p_1$: it is obtained from $p_n, \dots, p_1$ by deleting some of the entries.

results.title: Expected coalescent holding time
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: `E[T k] = (k.choose 2)⁻¹`.

results.title: Expected time to the most recent common ancestor
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The expected time to the most recent common ancestor is `2 (1 - 1/n)`.

results.title: Integrability of the total branch length
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The total branch length is integrable.

results.title: Expected total branch length of the coalescent
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The expected total branch length is `2 H_{n-1}`.

results.title: Variance of the time to the most recent common ancestor
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The variance of the time to the most recent common ancestor is `∑_{k=2}^n ((k.choose 2)⁻¹)²` (this uses independence).

results.title: Expected number of segregating sites
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Infinite-sites mutation at rate `θ/2` per lineage per unit time: if the number of segregating sites `S` is integrable and has conditional mean `(θ/2) L` given the genealogy σ-algebra `m`, then `E S = θ H_{n-1}`. (Integrability matters: Mathlib's conditional expectation of a non-integrable function is `0`.)

results.title: Integrability of Watterson's estimator
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Watterson's estimator `S / H_{n-1}` is integrable when `S` is.

results.title: Watterson's estimator is unbiased
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: `E[S / H_{n-1}] = θ` for a sample of size `n ≥ 2`.

results.title: Canonical probability space for Kingman holding times
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The canonical probability space for the Kingman holding times of a sample of size `n`: the product of the exponential laws `Exp (k.choose 2)`, `2 ≤ k ≤ n`.

results.title: Kingman coalescent from coordinate projections
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The coordinate projections of `piMeasure n` form a Kingman coalescent; in particular `KingmanTimes` is inhabited for every sample size.

results.title: Probability of no coalescence in one Wright–Fisher generation
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: In a Wright–Fisher population of `M` gene copies, the probability that `k` lineages, choosing their parents independently and uniformly, have `k` distinct parents.

results.title: No-coalescence probability as a falling factorial ratio
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: `noCoalProb M k` is the falling factorial `M (M-1) ⋯ (M-k+1)` divided by `M ^ k`.

results.title: No-coalescence probability tends to one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: `noCoalProb M k → 1` as `M → ∞`.

results.title: Kingman's coalescence rate
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `M` gene copies (`M = 2N`), the per-generation probability that some of `k` lineages coalesce is `(k.choose 2) / M + o(1/M)`; i.e. in time units of `M` generations, coalescences occur at rate `k.choose 2`.

results.title: Wright–Fisher coalescence times converge to exponential laws
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: After `⌊t M⌋` Wright–Fisher generations (`t ≥ 0` coalescent time units), the probability that `k` lineages have not coalesced tends to `exp (-(k.choose 2) t)`, the survival function of the exponential law with rate `k.choose 2`.
